newsitem.title: USA: NYS Bruno opens door to ending rent rules in 4 yrs.
newsitem.headline: NYS Bruno opens door to ending rent rules in 4 yrs.

text.p: The New York State Senate Majority Leader, who has gotten death threats for advocating ending rent controls, on Thursday opened the door to a longer transition to a free-market system than he first proposed.

Joseph Bruno, R-Troy, saying he had spoken with Republican senators who had suggested the two-year transition he had proposed was too short, speculated that a four-year transition--or perhaps even longer--might be better.

Asked by reporters if a four-year limit was a line in the sand, he replied: "It's not a line in the sand. It is an indication that I want to do what is responsible and reasonable as we transition out of rent control, and if four years helps us get there, then I'd be open to that."
Bruno spoke to reporters after a luncheon sponsored by the New York Building Congress, an association for design and construction professionals.

He has campaigned hard for ending state regulations setting apartment rents because he says they have made it uneconomic to build new apartments. The Building Congress, in a prepared release, said New York City is only adding 4,000 to 5,000 units a year, but needs to buld at least 20,000 to keep up with demand.

The Democrat-led Assembly wants to keep the present rent controls, which Bruno says he is willing to let expire on June 15 if no new pact is negotiated. The clash is one of the key issues holding up the state's budget, which was due April 1.

New York City has nearly one million rent-regulated apartments, the vast majority in the state, and Bruno defended himself from criticism that he should defer to the city's views on this issue. "What on earth does where I have to live have to do with what is right from wrong?"

While saying his position was more flexible than the Assembly, which approved a bill to make apartment rent controls permanent, Bruno made it plain he had not backed off his initial demand for a two-year transition.

"We opened our discussion with two-year transition, protecting the elderly, protecting the disabled, and protecting the lowest income, immediate vacancy decontrol, and lowering the luxury decontrol limits immediately from $250,000 to some number. That's our opener and that's where we are now."
Luxury decontrol rules set income limits on how much tenants can earn without losing rent-regulated apartments.

Bruno, explaining he wanted the present system of rules continued for the protected groups, also said that landlords should not have to automatically renew tenants' leases, adding he opposed letting rent-regulated apartments to be inherited.
